questions.q: According to the capstone brief, what should a commit history look like, rather than one giant initial commit?
options: It doesn't matter how commits are structured, as long as the final code works
Exactly one commit per file in the entire project
A history with no commit messages at all
A history of meaningful, individually reviewable commits that show real incremental work
questions.explain: The brief explicitly calls for meaningful, reviewable commits rather than dumping the whole project in one commit, mirroring how real collaborative projects are built.

questions.q: What does the brief require regarding merge conflicts?
options: At least one deliberate merge conflict should be created and actually resolved, not avoided
Conflicts should be avoided entirely by rewriting history around them
Merge conflicts are impossible in a single-person project, so this requirement doesn't apply
All conflicts must be resolved by deleting one branch entirely
questions.explain: The capstone specifically asks for a real, resolved merge conflict as proof the conflict-resolution skill from earlier in the course was actually exercised, not just read about.

questions.q: What does the brief ask you to document about your branching strategy choice?
options: A full diagram of every possible Git command
Nothing — branching strategy is irrelevant to the capstone
A written note stating whether the project uses Git Flow or trunk-based development, and why that fits a project of this size
A comparison of five different version control systems
questions.explain: The brief asks for a short, real justification of the chosen branching strategy, tying Chapter 3's concepts to an actual project decision.

questions.q: What must be true about the CI workflow's deploy job, according to the brief?
options: It must deploy before the tests even run
It should run on every single commit to every branch
It should never actually be configured, only described
It must be gated by github.event_name and github.ref so it only runs on a real merge to main
questions.explain: Consistent with Lesson 20, the deploy job must be conditioned to fire only on a real push/merge to main, not on every push or pull request.

questions.q: What does the brief mean by a 'vacuous pass' being something to avoid?
options: A tag created without a message
A pull request that gets approved without any review
A CI check that always succeeds because it isn't actually validating anything meaningful
A branch that was never merged
questions.explain: The lesson warns against wiring up CI before there's a real test or validation step for it to run, which produces a workflow that always passes without checking anything real.
